original_title: Pollo AI turns creative ideas into campaigns with OpenAI
original_summary: With GPT-5.6, GPT-6 Astra, and GPT‑Image‑2.5, Pollo AI helps creators turn bold ideas into detailed images and cinematic video ads.
article_content:
With GPT‑5.6, GPT‑6 Astra, and GPT‑Image‑2.5, Pollo AI helps creators turn bold ideas into detailed images and cinematic video ads.

Pollo AI⁠(opens in a new window) was founded on the premise that people should be able to turn their creative ideas into finished images and videos without needing production expertise. Even with generative AI, creators and marketers can struggle to navigate different tools and choose between models to get the result they want. Some may even abandon their projects in frustration.

“We want to do for video what Canva did for design. We want to make it easy enough that more people can actually use it, not just the ones who already know how,” explains Bill Zhu, the founder and CEO of Pollo AI. Today, Pollo AI serves more than 26 million users who use the platform to create videos, ads, and visual content.

The team’s first breakthrough was video templates. Now, 30% of creator sessions start from these templates or trending-format workflows. Building on this success, the company’s latest offering is Pollo Agent. It uses OpenAI models, including GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑Image‑2.5, to provide a fully guided workflow for video creation, including this post-apocalyptic adventure from a Pollo AI user.

Pollo Agent interprets the user’s rough ideas and visual references, and then develops storylines, scene flows, and scripts. CTO Peter Zhou says OpenAI models stood out for their ability to understand ambiguous creative inputs and their multimodal capability, sharing: “GPT‑5.6 performed especially well there.” The team also said they value the OpenAI API’s stability and release cadence.

To balance reasoning depth, speed, and cost, Pollo AI uses GPT‑5.6 for routing and GPT‑6 Astra for more challenging work, such as developing a narrative or planning scene revisions. This model mix lets the system match the level of reasoning to the task based on the user’s prompt. Pollo AI reports that users spend more than 50% less time choosing or switching models, giving them more time for creativity.

Pollo AI tests generative models against real user prompts and workflows, evaluating output quality, consistency, stylistic range, speed, and cost. GPT‑Image‑2.5 was selected to handle image generation, helping creators make posters, storyboards, and campaign visuals.

Pollo AI’s primary users are content creators, and the platform is especially popular for creating micro dramas with both AI and human actors. However, more marketers and business owners are starting to use Pollo AI to develop video content quickly and easily too.

Pollo’s Photo to Video Ads tool in its Marketing Studio suite uses OpenAI models to turn a still image and prompt into a short video. It’s designed to help small businesses and DTC brands generate product ads for social media in minutes rather than days.

One Pollo AI user wanted to use a product photo to make a fragrance ad that felt luxurious. The static photo alone could not convey that mood, and a professional video shoot was beyond their budget.

Using Photo to Video Ad, the user turned their starting image into a roughly 15-second video ad. The tool generated velvet textures, warm spotlights, and close-ups of the bottle to establish the mood across the sequence and ended it with the fragrance framed against deep red fabric.

Another customer, a jewelry brand, wanted a bold editorial campaign image, but its budget could not stretch to a high-concept studio shoot.

Using Pollo Agent and GPT‑Image‑2.5, the brand was able to turn its creative vision of its statement jewelry on a model seated beside a cheetah into reality. The tool framed the scene with dark drapery and warm lighting and ensured that the brand’s jewelry products were highly visible.

The customer got a finished luxury campaign visual with lower production effort, time, and cost compared to live shoot.

original_title: LegalOn halves Codex costs while maintaining development speed
original_summary: LegalOn cut estimated daily Codex costs by 65% while maintaining development speed. It matched Astra, Sol, and Luna to tasks and managed budgets strategically.
article_content:
LegalOn cut costs by 65% while maintaining development speed by matching Astra, Sol, and Luna to tasks and managing budgets strategically.

Cost reduction in mature business areas

Reduction in estimated daily costs

LegalOn Technologies offers Professional AI globally, using AI to support legal work and other key business functions. By combining domain expertise with AI, it enables people to focus on complex judgments and decisions. Its goal is AI-driven management that improves the quality and speed of business decision-making.

This approach extends beyond its products to making the organization itself AI-native. The company integrated Codex into its development process and expanded adoption across the organization through day-to-day use.

As adoption took hold, a new challenge emerged: cost control. Unlimited use of high-performance models could drive up spending, while blanket restrictions risked undermining the productivity gains AI had enabled.

How could it reduce costs without slowing development? LegalOn Technologies addressed this challenge by selecting among GPT‑6 (Astra, Luna) and GPT‑6.1 Sol based on task complexity and development stage, and aligning budgets with each business’s stage of growth. The company halved costs while maintaining development speed.

The company initially gave developers unlimited access to its main model, GPT‑5.5 in Fast mode. They expanded its use to design, implementation, and everyday work, learning through experimentation how best to divide responsibilities between people and AI.

Continuing to use high-performance models without limits, however, would inevitably exceed the annual budget. The company's AI-powered Development CoE (AID CoE) began developing guidelines for model selection. AID CoE tested and monitored models, while managers shared its findings with their teams. This enabled each engineer to independently choose the most suitable model for each task.

The new guidelines shifted the company from using the highest-capability model for every task to choosing the right model for the job. Teams started with a lightweight model and moved to more capable models as task complexity increased.

To support governance, the company also introduced system controls through administrator settings, with monthly usage limits for departments and individuals. AID CoE monitors usage and adjusts limits as business needs require.

Internal testing under these controls helped make the selection criteria more specific. GPT‑6 Luna, the lightest model, handles code implementation with clear requirements; GPT‑6.1 Sol supports standard design, data analysis, and document preparation; and GPT‑6 Astra, the most capable model, handles advanced judgment, including architecture design. Matching models to tasks gradually became a shared practice across teams.

Everyday execution and implementation; running everyday automations; delegating relatively simple tasks and analysis; code implementation, mainly as a subagent.

Standard design and analysis; relatively simple software design; routine numerical analysis and document creation; tasks requiring shorter completion times than with Luna.

Complex analysis, design, and orchestration; complex analysis and document creation; complex software design; coordinating agents as the orchestrator.

Alongside model selection, the company began restricting Fast mode by default, allowing individual requests only when needed. Although the change raised concerns about development speed, teams used approaches such as running tasks in parallel to maintain performance and transition smoothly.

It also introduced budget caps for AI spending at the department, group, and individual levels. The established LegalOn business was asked to improve cost efficiency by up to approximately 20%, while new businesses in the launch phase received generous budgets to encourage active use of AI.

original_title: Building on our commitment to American scientific discovery
original_summary: Building on our commitment to American scientific discovery
article_content:
Anthropic is deepening its support for American scientific research by committing $150 million over three years to the Genesis Mission, a federal initiative to accelerate scientific and technological discovery through AI. The funding will go toward making Claude available to more than 15 agencies that are part of the mission, including NASA, the National Institutes of Health, and the National Science Foundation.

We first announced our partnership with the US Department of Energy (DOE) and the Genesis Mission last December. Since then, we have worked with DOE to bring Claude to scientists across the national laboratories. Today, we announced this new commitment as part of the Science: A New Golden Age Summit hosted by the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy in Washington, DC.

We share the administration’s view, laid out in “Science: A New Golden Age,” that AI can have a profound and positive impact on scientific discovery, and we are glad to back its efforts to support American scientists.

Researchers at federal agencies and national laboratories work on some of the world’s most difficult scientific problems. Through our commitment, we aim to help them use Claude to meaningfully advance their work. Over the next three years, we will:

This commitment is part of our broader effort to support scientific research. Earlier this year we launched Claude Science, an AI workbench that integrates the tools and packages researchers most commonly use, and opened 10,000 free and discounted Claude seats for academic scientists. We also expanded our AI for Science program, which gives credits to researchers on high-impact projects, and kicked off a research preview of the Model Hardware Standard, a shared specification for AI agents to safely operate lab instruments. Our commitment to the Genesis Mission is our next step toward helping researchers everywhere.

We’re publishing a new version of our Usage Policy. In this post, we summarize the changes we’ve made.

We’re launching the Anthropic Cyber Mission, a long-term commitment to securing the systems everyone depends on.

We’re launching a new, expanded version of our Cyber Verification Program, which makes advanced cyber capabilities and reduced blocking classifiers available to qualifying security professionals.

original_title: Meta Donates 1,000 AI Glasses to Singapore’s Disability Community
original_summary:
Meta donates 1,000 Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses to four Singapore community organisations to help persons with disabilities.

The post Meta Donates 1,000 AI Glasses to Singapore’s Disability Community appeared first on Meta Newsroom.
article_content:
Today in Singapore, Joel Kaplan, Chief Global Affairs Officer at Meta, announced a donation of 1,000 Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses to the Singapore Association of the Visually Handicapped, Guide Dogs Singapore, the Singapore Disability Sports Council and Gardens by the Bay, alongside a US$30,000 investment into accessibility training.

We believe the future is for everyone. People use our Ray-Ban Meta glasses for everything from listening to music, to live translation and hands-free calls. But for persons with disabilities, the difference they make can be life-changing. For example, for people who are blind or have low vision, our AI glasses help with everyday tasks like reading text, identifying objects and describing the world around them, helping them regain their independence.

The announcement was made at an AI glasses accessibility showcase co-hosted by Meta and the Singapore Disability Sports Council (SDSC), with Guest-of-Honour Senior Parliamentary Secretary, Ministry of Law & Ministry of Social and Family Development Eric Chua and attendees from the disability community and the organisations that serve it, including SDSC athletes, Guide Dogs Singapore and SAVH, alongside officials working on digital inclusion.

Joel Kaplan said “The athletes and advocates I met today show what’s possible when technology is designed with independence in mind. I’ve seen firsthand how meaningful this technology is for people with disabilities. We believe the future is for everyone. That’s why, through our partnerships with the Singapore Association of the Visually Handicapped, Guide Dogs Singapore, the Singapore Disability Sports Council and Gardens by the Bay, we’re putting these glasses into the hands of the people who stand to benefit most.”

Dr Teo-Koh Sock Miang, President, Singapore Disability Sports Council, said: “This partnership is especially meaningful because Meta’s donation is more than a gift for today – it is an investment in a future where technology can expand possibilities for persons with disabilities. Whether fostering greater independence in daily life or enabling new ways to review training and enhance performance, its potential is significant. We are excited to see our community make this technology their own and discover innovative uses we have yet to imagine.”

Eric Chua, Senior Parliamentary Secretary, Ministry of Law & Ministry of Social and Family Development said: “When designed with persons with disabilities, Al and emerging technologies can improve quality of life and enable fuller participation in everyday life. Our goal is a Singapore where inclusion is not exceptional, but simply ordinary.”

Theresa Goh, Paralympian & National Para Shooter said: “Using the glasses hands-free has changed how I capture moments and stay connected through my day. Technology in the right hands has enormous potential for good, especially for the disabled community. We are grateful to Meta for helping our athletes and member organisations gain greater independence in their daily lives.”

Meta’s US$30,000 grant will support SAVH in developing and delivering a free accessibility curriculum, equipping persons with visual impairment in Singapore with practical skills to use the glasses safely and effectively in daily life. Training will cover identifying objects, reading text and using voice commands to support everyday tasks, enabling greater independence and participation.

Cheryl Yeo, Head of Rehabilitation Services, Singapore Association of the Visually Handicapped, said: “We are deeply grateful to Meta for sponsoring Meta AI glasses to SAVH and providing a grant to support accessibility training. This generous support empowers our visually impaired clients with greater independence and access to technology that enhances daily living. At the same time, SAVH plays a vital role in guiding responsible use, ensuring these devices are integrated safely and meaningfully into their lives. Together, we are building pathways toward inclusion,
